 Toyota's Twin-Turbo V6 Has A New Problem — Camshafts That Could Snap
 by 
 Michael Accardi 
 (IC: ) 
 Published:  November 16th, 2026 
 Share 
 Just when you thought Toyota was finally on top of the problems with its twin-turbo V6, the automaker announced another safety recall for an entirely new problem.
 Toyota has officially issued a voluntary safety recall covering approximately 62,000 non-hybrid Tundra pickups across the 2022–2023 and 2025–2026 model years. This time, it’s an improperly machined camshaft that could abruptly snap while driving.

 Casting a Wide Net for a Single Bad Batch
 Here is the good news — Toyota doesn't think all 62,000 trucks have a ticking time bomb under the hood.
 According to recall documentation and supplier tracking, the defect traces back to a single production lot from one specific supplier. Toyota estimates that only about 300 suspect camshafts made it out into the wild—each one installed on cylinder bank one. Because finding exactly which trucks have those camshafts requires a physical verification, the automaker is casting a wide net to make sure none slip through the cracks.
 Of note, the recall population skips a few major variants:
 Excluded: All i-FORCE MAX hybrid Tundra pickups
 Excluded: Toyota Sequoia SUVs equipped with the 3.4-liter twin-turbo V6
 Excluded: All 2024 model-year Tundra trucks
 Inspection and Replacement Timeline
 Toyota plans to notify affected owners by mid-January 2027. Once notified, owners will need to bring their pickups to an authorized dealership for a physical camshaft inspection. If technicians confirm a truck's bank-one camshaft came from the affected supplier batch, the dealer will install a replacement free of charge.
 Owners eager to check their status sooner can run their Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) at Toyota.com/recall or nhtsa.gov/recalls , or call the Toyota Brand Engagement Center at 1-800-331-4331.
 Another Chapter in the V35A-FTS Saga
 While this camshaft campaign is separate from earlier troubles, it's another rough chapter for Toyota’s V35A-FTS 3.4-liter twin-turbo V6.
 Since debuting in the redesigned 2022 Tundra, the powertrain has been dogged by three expansive recalls—covering more than 270,000 Tundra and Lexus LX vehicles—tied to manufacturing debris damaging the number-one main bearing. Toyota initially promised to drop brand-new replacement crate engines into every affected truck but has since pivoted to targeted testing to determine which engines actually require full replacement.
